headline: New Hampshire governor proposes last-dollar tuition aid for community college students
dek: Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s proposed program would cover eligible New Hampshire residents’ remaining tuition after other aid, but it still needs legislative approval for fall 2027.
body: New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte is proposing a state-funded tuition program for residents attending one of the state’s seven community colleges, offering a possible new path into training and higher education for families earning up to $100,000. The proposal, announced Oct. 14 at Manchester Community College, would begin in fall 2027 only if lawmakers approve it as part of the state budget. The [Community College System of New Hampshire’s announcement](https://www.ccsnh.edu/governor-announces-plan-for-community-college-promise-program/) describes the plan as a Community College Promise Program.

The proposal is a last-dollar grant, which means students would first use eligible federal and state grants and scholarships, with the state covering the remaining tuition balance. The program would not pay for fees, books, supplies, transportation, housing or other living expenses, according to the college system. That distinction is important: the plan could remove a tuition bill without making community college cost-free in the broader sense.

Eligibility would be tied to several conditions. Students would have to be New Hampshire residents admitted to a state community college, report total family income of no more than $100,000 with typical assets, submit the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, enroll in at least six credits per semester and maintain a 2.0 grade-point average while meeting federal satisfactory-progress rules. The system says both current and new students could qualify if the program takes effect.

The proposed benefit is aimed at a real but specific expense. [New Hampshire Bulletin](https://newhampshirebulletin.com/2026/10/14/ayotte-proposes-tuition-assistance-program-for-community-college-system/) reported that in-state community-college tuition is currently $238 per credit. Thirty credits, roughly a full academic year, would therefore cost $7,140 before other expenses. The Bulletin cited Community College System estimates putting total annual costs, including housing, transportation, books and personal expenses, between $22,000 and $28,000 depending on a student’s circumstances.

State officials estimate the new program would require about $5.5 million a year from the General Fund. That money would pay only the unpaid portion of tuition after other aid, so the final cost to the state would depend on how many eligible students enroll and how much federal and state assistance they already receive. The system’s official explanation says there would be no separate application for the Promise Program; financial-aid information would be used to determine eligibility if lawmakers approve it.

The proposal follows a separate tuition-waiver expansion by the University System of New Hampshire. [New Hampshire Public Radio](https://www.nhpr.org/education/2026-10-02/usnh-unh-plymouth-state-keene-state-tuition-waiver-higher-education-newhampshire) reported that the university system’s New Hampshire Promise program will cover tuition for qualifying first-year students and certain community-college transfers at UNH, Plymouth State, Keene State and an online UNH program. That system is using endowment funds and gifts, while the governor’s community-college plan would require state budget funding and legislative approval.

There is also a workforce argument behind the proposal. Community College System Chancellor Chuck Lloyd told the Bulletin that a $3 million pilot for Pell-eligible community-college students in 2023 produced a significant increase in recruitment. The proposed income ceiling would reach beyond the typical Pell-Grant population, potentially bringing in students who do not qualify for enough federal aid to make tuition manageable but still cannot easily absorb the cost.

The timing leaves several questions unresolved. Ayotte would need to win reelection to submit the budget proposal described by the college system, and the House and Senate would then have to approve the program during the 2027 budget process. The system says that process is expected to begin early next year and conclude by June 30, 2027. Until those decisions are made, eligible students should treat the Promise Program as a proposal rather than an available benefit.
